newsitem.title: USA: Coronary heart disease down but still top killer.
newsitem.headline: Coronary heart disease down but still top killer.

text.p: Deaths from coronary heart disease are falling but the rate of decline of the leading killer in the United States has been slower in the 1990s than in previous decades, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the rate of coronary heart disease deaths declined 2.6 percent per year in the 1990s. The decrease averaged 3.0 percent per year during the 1980s.

The CDC said coronary heart disease, which accounts for two-thirds of all heart disease, was the most frequent cause of death in the United States, with 481,458 in 1994. About 57 million Americans, about one-fourth of the population, live with some form of heart disease.

The largest declines in coronary heart disease deaths occurred among whites and men. The average annual decrease among white men was 2.9 percent per year. For black women, it was 1.6 percent per year.

"Given the economic inequalities that exist between blacks and whites in the United States, it is possible that many of the prevention efforts are not reaching large segments of the black population," CDC epidemiologist Michele Casper said.

There was a large variation in death rates among the states with the Northeast and Midwest generally having higher death rates than the West. New York had the highest death rates from coronary heart disease -- 638.8 per 100,000 men and 406.3 per 100,000 women.

Health experts said Americans could prevent heart disease by eating heart-healthy foods, not using tobacco and engaging in physical activity. Better prevention of high cholesterol, hypertension and diabetes would also help, the CDC said.

A 1988 study in 37 states found a correlation between coronary heart disease deaths and being physically inactive. A 1960 study in 44 states found per capita cigarette sales were directly linked to deaths from coronary heart disease.

A study earlier this week said most of the recent decline in deaths from coronary heart disease has occurred because of improved management of patients. Researchers said in the Journal of the American Medical Association that only about 25 percent of the decline in deaths occurred because people were taking better care of themselves.
